lessons.title: Write ม, า, น, and ำ
lessons.description: Start with a tiny set that already lets you write useful words.

intro.whatThisIs: A consonant is the main letter shape in a Thai syllable. A vowel changes the sound around it.
intro.howItBehaves: ม and น sit on the writing line. า sits after the consonant, while ำ sits above and after it as one vowel package.
intro.whyItMatters: These four symbols already unlock come, bring, and water.
intro.example: มา is ม + า.

lessons.title: Bridge into real words
lessons.description: Use the first symbols immediately in small, high-value words.

intro.whatThisIs: A word bridge turns fresh symbols into complete Thai words right away.
intro.howItBehaves: Transliteration is only a rough Latin guide. The Thai spelling is the real target you are learning to write.
intro.whyItMatters: You should see useful Thai before the course starts to feel abstract.
intro.example: นำ is น + ำ.

lessons.title: Add บ, แ, and the first tone marks
lessons.description: Pick up one common consonant, one front vowel, and the first two marks written above the stack.

intro.whatThisIs: Tone marks are small marks that sit above a consonant and change how the word sounds.
intro.howItBehaves: แ is written before the consonant, even though you still say the consonant first. ่ and ้ sit above the consonant stack.
intro.whyItMatters: This gives you home and family words almost immediately.
intro.example: แม่ uses แ before ม and ่ above the stack.

lessons.title: Home, family, and not
lessons.description: Build words that matter early, even if one especially useful piece arrives a lesson later.

intro.whatThisIs: Build words use only symbols you already know. Preview words add one missing feature and label it clearly.
intro.howItBehaves: If one part is marked coming soon, copy the whole word now and let the next lesson explain that last piece.
intro.whyItMatters: บ้าน, แม่, and ไม่ show you how Thai words start coming together.
intro.example: ไม่ is mostly familiar already; the front vowel ไ is the only new piece.

lessons.title: Add พ, อ, ไ, and ป
lessons.description: Learn another family consonant, the carrier letter, a front vowel, and a common action consonant.

intro.whatThisIs: อ can be a real consonant, but it also works as the carrier that helps you see where dependent vowels and tone marks sit.
intro.howItBehaves: ไ is written before the consonant. อ is the placeholder you practice with when a vowel or tone mark cannot stand alone.
intro.whyItMatters: This batch unlocks father, go, and enough.
intro.example: ไป is ไ before ป.

lessons.title: Father, go, and enough
lessons.description: Use the new front vowel and carrier right away in short everyday words.

intro.whatThisIs: These are full build words, so every part now has a matching symbol lesson behind it.
intro.howItBehaves: Watch how อ sometimes carries a vowel sound at the end of a word instead of acting like a simple consonant.
intro.whyItMatters: You can already write go, father, enough, house, mother, not, bring, water, and come.
intro.example: พอ is พ + อ.

lessons.title: Add ใ, ะ, ั, and ก
lessons.description: Finish the beginner utility marks that make Thai function words much easier to read and write.

intro.whatThisIs: ใ is a second ai vowel used in a smaller set of words. ะ and ั give short a sounds.
intro.howItBehaves: ใ is written before the consonant. ะ is written after it. ั sits above the consonant to make a short a sound inside the word.
intro.whyItMatters: These marks power words like ใน, กับ, and ครับ.
intro.example: กับ uses ก + ั + บ.

lessons.title: Add ค, ด, ต, and ย
lessons.description: These high-utility consonants expand the range of useful short words quickly.

intro.whatThisIs: This is still the utility track, so the letters here are chosen for everyday payoff instead of official alphabet order.
intro.howItBehaves: Thai keeps multiple letters for similar sounds. Learn the shape first; the fine sound-class details can come later.
intro.whyItMatters: This batch unlocks polite particles and the common word ได้.
intro.example: ได้ uses ด with the front vowel ไ and the tone mark ้.

lessons.title: Inside, with, polite, can
lessons.description: These short utility words show why the early symbol order is built around usefulness.

intro.whatThisIs: This bridge focuses on glue words and polite speech rather than names or trivia.
intro.howItBehaves: Notice how Thai writes short hidden vowels with marks like ั instead of always adding a full vowel letter.
intro.whyItMatters: Words like ใน, กับ, ค่ะ, and ได้ appear constantly.
intro.example: ค่ะ is ค + ่ + ะ.

lessons.title: Add ล, ว, ร, and ห
lessons.description: These letters help you form everyday polite words, question words, and connectors.

intro.whatThisIs: You are still in the common-letter track, where every new shape should pay off in real words soon.
intro.howItBehaves: ว often works with vowels or ends a syllable. ห sometimes shapes tone even when its sound is quiet.
intro.whyItMatters: These letters unlock polite particles like ครับ and question words like ไหน.
intro.example: แล้ว uses แ before ล and ends with ว.

lessons.title: Add ข, จ, ส, and ท
lessons.description: Round out another practical layer of the common alphabet before the later completion block.

intro.whatThisIs: These are still common everyday letters, even if they arrive later than the official alphabet would suggest.
intro.howItBehaves: Some of these letters share sound territory with symbols you already know, so keep the shape and word examples tied together.
intro.whyItMatters: They let you write request words, questions, and more common sentence glue.
intro.example: ขอ is ข + อ.

lessons.title: Please, already, where
lessons.description: Add more survival-basic words before you fill out the rest of the alphabet.

intro.whatThisIs: This bridge leans on question words, request words, and polite particles you can use in real conversation.
intro.howItBehaves: Thai often hides short vowels inside compact spellings, so keep breaking each word into parts instead of guessing from sound alone.
intro.whyItMatters: ครับ, ขอ, แล้ว, and ไหน are all strong beginner payoffs.
intro.example: ครับ is ค + ร + ั + บ.

lessons.title: Upper and lower vowel marks
lessons.description: Now that the first useful words are in motion, fill in more of the common vowel inventory.

intro.whatThisIs: These vowels sit above or below the consonant instead of before or after it.
intro.howItBehaves: You still practice them with the carrier อ so the placement stays obvious.
intro.whyItMatters: They appear everywhere once you move beyond the tiny starter vocabulary.
intro.example: อิ shows the mark above the carrier.

lessons.title: More frame vowels and tone marks
lessons.description: Finish the remaining common starter vowels and the last two tone marks.

intro.whatThisIs: เ and โ are frame vowels that wrap around the consonant pattern, and ๊ / ๋ complete the four tone marks.
intro.howItBehaves: Frame vowels are written around the consonant frame, not simply after it.
intro.whyItMatters: You do not need these on day one, but they round out the system before the final alphabet cleanup.
intro.example: เอ puts เ before the carrier and อ after it.

lessons.title: Add ง, ถ, ธ, and ฟ
lessons.description: Keep filling in common reading letters before the rare completion block starts.

intro.whatThisIs: These letters are less urgent than the first utility track, but they still matter much earlier than the rare historic forms.
intro.howItBehaves: Several of these overlap in sound with letters you already know, so anchor them by shape and example words.
intro.whyItMatters: This keeps the practical reading alphabet growing without front-loading the rare letters.
intro.example: ง is especially common at the end of a syllable.

lessons.title: Add ผ, ฝ, ฮ, and ซ
lessons.description: Pick up the remaining practical letters that still show up in everyday reading.

intro.whatThisIs: This batch finishes another slice of the common alphabet before the low-utility cleanup lessons.
intro.howItBehaves: Some letters here overlap in sound, but their shapes and word families are different.
intro.whyItMatters: You will meet these in everyday names, signs, and loanwords sooner than the rare historical letters.
intro.example: ฮ often appears in modern or borrowed words.

lessons.title: Add ภ, ฆ, ญ, and ช
lessons.description: Finish the rest of the still-usable core set before you switch to alphabet completion.

intro.whatThisIs: These are not the first letters a beginner needs, but they still appear often enough to learn before the rare block.
intro.howItBehaves: Thai keeps several historical consonants with overlapping sounds, so treat shape recognition as the main job first.
intro.whyItMatters: Once these are in place, the remaining lessons can focus on official-alphabet completion.
intro.example: ช is common enough that you will notice it quickly in everyday reading.

lessons.title: Rare kha and retroflex forms
lessons.description: Now fill in low-utility official letters without asking a beginner to memorize them first.

intro.whatThisIs: This block is about finishing the official Thai alphabet, not about front-loading beginner usefulness.
intro.howItBehaves: Several of these letters are rare or historical. You still need the official shapes for full literacy.
intro.whyItMatters: You can now learn them after the practical track is already doing real work.
intro.example: ฃ and ฅ are rare today, but they are still part of the official set.

lessons.title: More rare official letters
lessons.description: Continue the cleanup pass through the low-frequency historic forms.

intro.whatThisIs: These letters matter for complete alphabet coverage, but not for the opening utility path.
intro.howItBehaves: You may hear sounds here that overlap with common letters you already know.
intro.whyItMatters: The goal is confident recognition and writing of the full official inventory.
intro.example: ฏ and ฐ are official letters even if they are not day-one priorities.

lessons.title: Finish the official set
lessons.description: Close out the remaining low-utility letters after the useful track is already stable.

intro.whatThisIs: This last block completes the full alphabet without pretending these were the best opening lessons for a complete beginner.
intro.howItBehaves: Keep using the same writing-first process: see the shape, copy it cleanly, then bring it back later through review.
intro.whyItMatters: You finish with full coverage while keeping the first half of the course practical.
intro.example: ศ, ษ, ฬ, and ฌ are all official letters, even if they are not high-frequency beginner wins.
